extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on peer-review systems, conference organizers, and machine learning/AI researchers interested in bidding/assignment algorithms
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating algorithms that order papers shown to sequentially arriving reviewers to optimize bidding outcomes in conference peer review. Focus is on balancing per-paper bid coverage and reviewer satisfaction while accounting for ordering/primacy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining sufficiently many bids for each paper
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding on the ordering of papers to show, one competing goal is obtaining sufficiently many bids for each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance metric: reduce the number of papers with fewer than requisite bids. Empirical claim from the paper: SUPER* consistently reduces the number of such papers by 50-75% or more compared to baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfying reviewers by showing them relevant items
rubrics_metrics.description: The other competing goal is satisfying reviewers by showing them relevant items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer satisfaction is operationalized by showing reviewers papers relevant to their interests/expertise; an ordering should prioritize relevance to maintain reviewer engagement and quality of bids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for primacy effects (order has significant impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of the papers shown has a significant impact on the bids due to primacy effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm design must model sequential arrival and primacy bias — earlier-positioned items receive more attention/bids. Ignoring primacy leads to suboptimal bid distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing a principled framework to study the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by developing a framework to study this problem in a principled manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: formal model that captures sequential reviewer arrivals, relevance/similarity, and bidding behavior so that algorithms can be analyzed theoretically and empirically under clear assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local optimality guarantee for the ordering algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an algorithm called SUPER*, inspired by the A* algorithm, and theoretically show a local optimality guarantee of the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric: provide provable guarantees (e.g., local optimality) about the algorithm's behavior. Theoretical analysis should justify algorithmic choices and show improvement over naive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Near-optimality under a community model for similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a community model for the similarities, prove that SUPER* is near-optimal whereas the popular baselines are considerably suboptimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric: analyze algorithm performance under realistic generative models (here, a community model) and demonstrate near-optimality relative to an objective; contrast with baseline guarantees (or lack thereof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation on real and synthetic data, including robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: In experiments on real data from ICLR 2018 and synthetic data, SUPER* considerably outperforms baselines deployed in existing systems and is also robust to various real world complexities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric: evaluate on both real conference data and synthetic simulations, report metrics (e.g., number of under-bidded papers), and test robustness to modeling mismatches and other practical complexities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to popular baselines and demonstrate their suboptimality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that popular baselines are considerably suboptimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubric: include theoretical and empirical comparisons to existing/baseline ordering or bidding strategies to demonstrate superiority; explicitly identify baseline algorithms used in deployed systems.
